html:
In 1907 Pablo Picasso saw African masks and carvings in Paris, and they shaped his painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, the work that opened the way to Cubism.

Objects from Africa and Oceania had been flowing into Paris along with France's colonial conquests. Artists hunted for them in junk shops, and the ethnographic museum at the Trocadéro displayed them. Henri Matisse and André Derain were already collecting African sculpture, and Matisse showed a piece to Picasso.

That summer Picasso visited the Trocadéro museum, an experience he later described as a revelation. He went back to the Demoiselles, a large painting of five nude women, and repainted the faces of the two figures on the right as harsh, mask-like shapes with hatched lines. The left figures draw more on ancient Iberian sculpture.

The painting shocked even his friends. Together with Georges Braque, Picasso went on to break forms into flat planes. African art, valued in Paris for its forms rather than its meaning, became part of the story of modern art. Today people also ask how those objects reached Europe; compare the Benin Bronzes, looted in 1897.
sum: In 1907 Pablo Picasso saw African masks and carvings in Paris, and they shaped his painting Les Demoiselles d'Avignon, the work that opened the way to Cubism.
